# Choosing items to predict a model's full-benchmark score: code and results

Code, protocol and result tables for the study of how to choose `n ≪ N` benchmark items for a target model and predict its full-benchmark score from the item-level results of other ("source") models. Thirteen binary item × model matrices (7 Open LLM Leaderboard v2, 6 HELM), three target splits (random models, held-out model families, models above every source), seven item-selection designs, about a hundred predictor/estimator combinations.

Contents

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `src/bpred/` | library: data loading and de-duplication (`data.py`), designs, predictors, estimators, adaptive CAT (`core.py`) |
| `scripts/` | experiments and analyses, numbered in execution order (below); `run_all.sh` runs everything on one machine |
| `PROTOCOL.md` | the protocol, written before any target was scored, with the log of later deviations |
| `RESULTS_SCHEMA.md` | every file in `results/`, its columns, and how to read a method name |
| `REPRODUCE.md` | commands, seeds, compute budget, script → table/figure map |
| `REPRO_NOTES.md` | disclosure of an exposure to reserved material (read it) |
| `results/` | all aggregate CSVs behind the paper's numbers (~8 MB); raw per-draw predictions are too large for the repository (see "Raw outputs") |

## Environment

Python 3.11; numpy 2.4.6, scipy 1.17.1, pandas 3.0.6, scikit-learn 1.9.1, torch 2.14.1 (CPU build), joblib 1.6.0, pyarrow 26.0.0 (`requirements.txt`). No GPU. The scripts set `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=OMP_NUM_THREADS=MKL_NUM_THREADS=1`; keep BLAS single-threaded (multi-threaded BLAS made the small eigen-decompositions 10× slower on a shared machine). Peak memory of one worker < 6 GB.

## Data

`scripts/00_download.sh` downloads the 13 score matrices and model lists from a public repository at a pinned commit (`55faff496947789f94e6b5908c77cbc3e84f81ad` of `socialfoundations/benchmark-prediction`; ~80 MB) into `data/raw/` and writes `SHA256SUMS`. The data are **not** bundled here. Only the binary item-level outcomes (and model names, used to derive families) are used; no benchmark text, no code of that repository. The source repository states an MIT licence; the licences of the benchmark datasets whose outcomes the matrices record (Open LLM Leaderboard v2 tasks, HELM scenarios) were not individually verified, which is one reason the matrices are fetched rather than redistributed. `python3 scripts/01_audit.py` writes the audit (`results/audit.csv`): models, duplicates dropped, constant items, families.

## 0. The paper in one paragraph
Evaluating an LLM on a full benchmark is costly, so we run it on n ≪ N items and predict its full score. Existing methods (anchor points, tinyBenchmarks, metabench, assessor, active acquisition) use the score matrix of *source models* to pick items and fit a *latent model* of the target; they are judged mostly on held-out models that resemble the sources. We cast the problem as **finite-population estimation of a mean of N unknown 0/1 values with a free covariate (the source matrix)**. That frame separates what the sources can buy — **variance reduction** — from what must be controlled by design — **bias**. We (i) test, on 13 binary matrices and under three target splits (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage-held-out), whether model-based predictors lose accuracy where targets differ from the sources; (ii) test whether a design-based correction (probability sampling with a positivity floor + difference/GREG estimator) repairs it and at what variance cost; (iii) measure how much the source matrix can help at all over plain stratified/balanced random sampling; (iv) examine ordering of models separately from score error.
